paper_title: Beyond Memory: Harnessing Long-Horizon Agents with Explicit Belief States

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language model (LLM) agents can now undertake increasingly complex tasks, but the way they organize interaction history into memory does not ensure a coherent understanding of the current world. We introduce PoS, an inference-time framework that constructs and continually maintains explicit belief states as the agent's decision context. Each belief combines an estimate of the current world state with unresolved task requirements, making explicit what the agent still needs to learn and accomplish. To keep this belief reliable and actionable, PoS validates its consistency and monitors task progress to detect Belief Trapping, where the agent continues to act without making meaningful progress toward the goal. Recovery is then tailored to both the trapping pattern and the type of unresolved task requirement. Experiments on four benchmarks spanning execution and diagnosis show that PoS achieves the highest overall performance on every benchmark with all three LLM backbones. Ablations demonstrate the importance of consistency validation and recovery, while context-scaling experiments show resilience to context growth. Together, these results support belief construction and continual maintenance as a foundation for long-horizon context management beyond history retention and compression.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: LLM agents are increasingly equipped with ultra-long context windows (Yang et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026a; Hu et al., 2026), stronger reasoning and tool-use capabilities (Guo et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2026), external memory systems (Hu et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026b), and sophisticated execution harnesses (Ma et al., 2026; Wan et al., 2026), substantially expanding the complexity and horizon of tasks they can undertake. However, longer interaction horizons expose deeper challenge, as actions may alter the environment and new observations may invalidate earlier inferences. Accumulated context thus mixes evidence about past states with intermediate judgments, making it increasingly difficult to identify which facts still hold, which inferences remain supported, and what remains unresolved. Raw trajectories preserve this evidence chronologically, while memory mechanisms select, compress, or reorganize it. While both are valuable, access to evidence alone does not ensure an explicit and coherent estimate of the current world that can be revised and checked across steps. Recent work observes that when task state remains implicit within growing context, outdated or inconsistent information can persist across subsequent decisions (Ma et al., 2026). The next barrier to reliable long-horizon LLM agents is therefore not simply retaining more history, but maintaining an actionable representation of the current world. formal basis for this representation is the belief state 𝑏𝑡 (𝑠) = 𝑃(𝑠𝑡 = 𝑠 ℎ𝑡 ), the posterior over the current latent world state 𝑠𝑡 given interaction history ℎ𝑡 . In standard partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), this belief is sufficient statistic for decision-making and can be recursively updated after each action and observation (Kaelbling et al., 1998). Recent methods have begun to explicitly represent the belief state through goal-relative reflection, probabilistic hypotheses, structured graphs, or audited task records (Kim et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026). Such representations make the agents current understanding of the world available for inspection and revision. However, explicit belief construction is just the start, as an LLM-generated belief must satisfy two further requirements. First, belief updates must remain internally consistent and supported by interaction evidence. Since these updates are generated by the LLM itself, they may introduce conflicting states or unsupported inferences that undermine subsequent decisions and ultimately lead to task failure. For instance, recording microwave as both open and closed makes it unclear whether the robot should open it before placing mug inside. Continual validation is thus essential to sustain the coherence and evidential support of the evolving belief state. Second, consistency alone does not prevent the failure mode we term Belief Trapping, where the agent continues to act without making meaningful progress toward the goal. For example, the agent may repeat ineffective actions, cycle through previously visited states, or gather information that does not help complete the task. Unproductive interactions will exhaust the available budget before achieving the goal, making timely detection and recovery necessary to restore meaningful task progress. T3 detects belief deviation and truncates uninformative trajectories for reinforcement learning, but does not provide recovery strategy within the ongoing episode (Zou et al., 2026). To our knowledge, no existing framework maintains belief state with both continual consistency validation and online diagnosis and recovery from Belief Trapping. We introduce Progression of States (PoS), unified framework that integrates explicit belief modeling, consistency validation, and trapping-aware recovery for long-horizon agent decision-making. As illustrated in Figure 2, PoS continually updates world state of task-relevant Entities, States, and Relations, along with epistemic and achievement gaps that specify what the agent still needs to learn or accomplish. The agent selects actions from the current belief, while Belief Sentinel validates updates for internal consistency and support from interaction evidence. PoS also assesses whether belief evolution supports continued task progress using three measures: gap persistence, progress stagnation, and belief recurrence. It then performs factorized trapping diagnosis along two dimensions, agent dynamics and blocked gap type, and composes corresponding recovery constraints to recover from Belief Trapping. We evaluate PoS using three LLM backbones on ALFWorld and LOCA-Bench for execution tasks and RCA-100 and ClinDiag for diagnosis tasks. PoS achieves the highest overall performance on all four benchmarks with each backbone, with relative gains over the strongest baseline reaching 22.68% on ALFWorld and 37.89% on RCA-100 joint accuracy. Ablation studies demonstrate the importance of consistency validation and trapping recovery beyond explicit belief construction. Further analyses examine trapping patterns and recovery effectiveness, robustness to context growth, and the tradeoff between token consumption and task performance.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: We organize prior approaches to long-horizon context management according to the decision context they expose to the agent: memory as context and belief as context.

sections.title: 2.1 Memory as Context
sections.content: ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) provides foundational framework for LLM agents, conditioning each action on the growing raw interaction trajectory. Compression-based methods instead summarize accumulated context into compact forms: ReadAgent (Lee et al., 2024) constructs retrievable gist memories, ACON (Kang et al., 2025) optimizes guidelines for history compression, and SUPO (Lu et al., 2026) jointly learns periodic summarization and tool-use policies. Other methods impose structure on the retained context: HiAgent (Hu et al., 2025) organizes working memory around subgoals, COMPASS (Wan et al., 2026) maintains concise progress briefs across reasoning stages, and PACE (Wei et al., 2026) adjusts historical granularity according to its predicted relevance to the next action. Other approaches make context management itself an agent-controlled operation: MemGPT manages information across in-context and external memory through an operating-system-inspired hierarchy (Packer et al., 2023). CaT (Liu et al., 2026) exposes context compression as callable tool over structured workspace, AgentFold (Ye et al., 2026) performs proactive multi-scale folding of historical trajectories, and Sculptor (Li et al., 2026) provides explicit tools for actively curating the working context. Although these methods improve evidence accessibility and context efficiency, the resulting context remains transformed record of historical evidence rather than consistent estimate of the current world.

sections.title: 2.2 Belief as Context
sections.content: A parallel line of work studies how LLMs represent the current state of an evolving world (Gurnee and Tegmark, 2024). Mechanistic studies probe the world-state abstractions encoded by LLMs (Li et al., 2024) and show that state tracking of reasoning is itself learned computation whose underlying mechanism affects systematic generalization (Li et al., 2025). Agent frameworks further externalize parts of this computation (Tang et al., 2024). QuBE (Kim et al., 2024) constructs task-relevant belief through question answering; StateAct (Rozanov and Rei, 2025) maintains chain of states throughout task execution; and ReflAct (Kim et al., 2025) grounds action selection in reflection over the current state relative to the goal. More structured approaches maintain particle beliefs over latent states and goals through hypothesis trees and Bayesian filtering (Tang et al., 2026), recursively update natural-language belief summaries (Lidayan et al., 2025), or combine causal graphs with state machines as explicit belief (Luo et al., 2026). LongHorizon-Harness (Ma et al., 2026) externalizes task state as audited records of requirements, artifacts, and facts, preserving verified progress through Manage-Execute-Audit loop. However, it relies on independently verifiable intermediate results and is therefore less suitable when meaningful progress consists of uncertain inferences rather than observable outcomes. Beyond belief construction, recent work has also begun to address failure modes related to Belief Trapping. T3 (Zou et al., 2026) detects excessive belief deviation and truncates uninformative trajectories during reinforcement learning, while CGDP (Kausik et al., 2026) uses an exhaustion gate to terminate unproductive context gathering. These approaches address stalled progress through truncation or termination, without attempting to restore progress during inference. In contrast, PoS maintains and validates task-conditioned belief and uses factorized recovery to redirect subsequent actions.

sections.title: 4.1 Main Results
sections.content: (1) Existing context management does not consistently improve upon raw trajectories. Table 1 reveals substantial variation in baseline performance across tasks and backbones. PACE remains competitive on ALFWorld and RCA100, but falls 24.5728.19 points below Raw Trajectory on LOCA-Bench. LongHorizon-Harness performs well on LOCA-Bench, where explicit requirements and generated artifacts support intermediate verification, but delivers less consistent gains on RCA-100 and ClinDiag, as progress depends on refining uncertain diagnostic hypotheses rather than producing directly verifiable artifacts. On ClinDiag with GLM-5.3, none of the context-management baselines outperforms Raw Trajectory. These reversals suggest that additional compression and organization do not consistently benefit modern LLMs with strong long-context capabilities, as information loss may offset the benefits of reducing redundancy. In contrast, PoS achieves (2) PoS consistently outperforms existing methods across diverse tasks and backbones. the highest overall performance on all four benchmarks under all three backbones. Compared with the strongest baseline with the same backbone, PoS achieves relative gains of up to 22.68% on ALFWorld, 7.53% on LOCA-Bench, 7 37.89% on RCA-100 joint accuracy, and 11.31% on ClinDiag. The gains span both execution and diagnosis tasks, indicating that they are not tied to particular task structure. These results highlight the importance of maintaining an accurate, task-conditioned belief about the current world state and unresolved requirements, beyond retaining and organizing interaction history. (3) Effective belief modeling requires maintaining both consistency and health. Removing Consistency Validation lowers performance across all four benchmarks to varying degrees, with losses reaching 14.93 points on ALFWorld and 11.81 points on LOCA-Bench, compared with 0.330.66 points on ClinDiag. This pattern is consistent with the greater risk of inconsistent belief updates when complex interactions require the agent to reconcile changing states and observations across steps. Removing Trapping Diagnosis and its associated recovery also degrades performance across all four benchmarks, including losses of 4.856.79 points on RCA-100 and 2.653.97 points on ClinDiag. Recovery complements validation by redirecting actions toward unresolved requirements when continued interaction no longer advances the task. Together, these results demonstrate the value of maintaining both belief consistency and task progress, beyond constructing an explicit representation.

sections.title: 4.2 Belief Trapping Analysis
sections.content: Figure 3: Belief Trapping and recovery across benchmarks. Left: Percentage of episodes with detected trapping under each backbone. Middle: Distribution of trapping patterns by benchmark. Right: Final task performance over all evaluated cases with Qwen3.7-Plus, comparing PoSs factorized recovery with generic recovery prompt. Figure 3 summarizes detected trapping incidence (left), the distribution of trapping patterns (middle), and the effect of recovery strategies after trapping is detected (right). It reveals that trapping is common across different settings, although stronger backbones generally exhibit lower incidence. However, lower trapping incidence does not necessarily imply higher final accuracy: on RCA-100, Kimi-K3 exhibits more trapping than GLM-5.3 (74% vs. 53%) but achieves higher Joint accuracy  (Table 1)  . The dominant trapping pattern also varies across benchmarks, with cycles most frequent in ALFWorld, drift in LOCA-Bench and RCA-100 (55.93%), and static stagnation in ClinDiag (78.25%). These differences reflect how unproductive interactions affect belief transition. Embodied actions may revisit prior states, multisource evidence may update beliefs without advancing the active gap, and non-discriminative clinical investigations may leave diagnostic beliefs unchanged. To assess the value of factorized recovery, we compare PoS with variant that replaces factorized recovery constraints with generic prompt asking the agent to recover. Figure 3 (right) shows that PoSs recovery strategy outperforms this variant across all four benchmarks. These results demonstrate that effective recovery goes beyond interrupting unproductive behavior, with factorized recovery tailored to the trapping dynamics and blocked gap type.

sections.title: 4.3 Cost–Performance Tradeoff
sections.content: Table 2 examines the costperformance tradeoff on RCA-100 with Qwen3.7-Plus. Compared with Raw Trajectory, PoS improves joint accuracy from 24.27% to 38.83%, while reducing Task Agent token consumption by 20.9%. However, total consumption increases to 5.06, as additional computation is devoted to belief construction and maintenance. Removing Consistency Validation substantially reduces Sentinel overhead and saves 35.6% of total tokens, but sacrifices 7.76 points in joint accuracy. sections.title: 4.4 Scaling under Context Growth
sections.content: Figure 4: Success rates on LOCA-Bench as context grows from 8K to 256K across backbones. Figure 4 compares task success on LOCA-Bench as environment descriptions grow from 8K to 256K across three backbones. Although performance generally declines with context length, ACON shows more gradual decline than Raw Trajectory at longer contexts. By compressing accumulated interaction history whenever the context exceeds predefined threshold, ACON reduces redundancy, whose increasing burden can make compression beneficial despite potential information loss. Meanwhile, PoS maintains broadly stable performance from 96K to 256K, exceeding the strongest baseline by 10.6716.00 points at 256K. By integrating new observations into an existing world state and unresolved requirements, PoS grounds each decision in the current task conditions rather than requiring the agent to reconstruct them from an increasingly long interaction history. This incremental maintenance reduces repeated interpretation of dispersed or outdated observations, while consistency validation and progress monitoring help prevent unsupported updates and stalled interactions from persisting. Together, these results suggest that effective context management should balance reducing historical redundancy with maintaining reliable and actionable understanding of the current world.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: In this work, we showed that explicit belief construction alone is insufficient for reliable long-horizon decision-making. We proposed PoS, framework that constructs task-conditioned belief states and continually maintains them through consistency validation and factorized recovery from Belief Trapping. Experiments across four benchmarks and three LLM backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in execution and diagnosis, together with resilience to context growth. Although PoS uses more tokens, the resulting gains demonstrate the potential of investing inference-time computation in belief maintenance. Reducing this overhead while preserving the gains in agent performance is an important direction for future work.

sections.title: D Implementation and Reproducibility Details
sections.content: D.1 Backbone and Agent Configuration We evaluate all methods with three backbone models: Qwen3.7-Plus, Kimi-K3, and GLM-5.3. The model is accessed through the DashScope OpenAI-compatible API (https://dashscope.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1); no fixed API snapshot is available. For each backbone setting, all LLM-based components of PoS and baselines use the same backbone as the corresponding baseline agents. We do not use stronger auxiliary model for belief construction, validation, or trapping-aware recovery. The Task Agent selects its action from the current task-conditioned belief state, which serves as its decision context. The only model fixed independently of the evaluated backbone occurs in the medical diagnosis benchmark ClinDiag. Its provider and judge are treated as part of the benchmark environment rather than as components of the evaluated 21 agent. To keep this environment identical across backbone settings, both are implemented with Qwen3.7-plus for all methods and backbones. All agent-side model calls use deterministic decoding with temperature 0. We set the maximum generation length to 512 tokens for ALFWorld, where each interaction primarily requires selecting an environment action, and to 4096 tokens for LOCA-Bench, RCA-100, and ClinDiag. D.2 Baseline Selection We select baselines to cover representative forms of decision context while remaining applicable under common cross-domain evaluation setting. Raw Trajectory serves as the uncompressed reference and exposes the complete interaction history directly to the Agent. Among memory-based approaches, ACON (Kang et al., 2025), PACE (Wei et al., 2026), and HiAgent (Hu et al., 2025) represent complementary strategies based on history compression, adaptive context granularity, and hierarchical subgoal-oriented working memory, respectively. We further include LongHorizonHarness (Ma et al., 2026) as closely related state-oriented baseline because it explicitly maintains an audited task state across long-horizon execution. Together, these methods span raw history, compressed and selectively retained context, hierarchical memory, and explicit task-state maintenance, while remaining adaptable to the same four evaluation environments and backbone settings. We do not attempt to exhaustively benchmark every method discussed in Section 2, as several approaches differ substantially in their training assumptions, control architecture, or task-specific state representation. For example, SUPO (Lu et al., 2026) jointly optimizes summarization and tool-use policies through reinforcement learning, while CaT (Liu et al., 2026) and AgentFold (Ye et al., 2026) rely on learned policies for actively manipulating the working context. Several belief-oriented methods are likewise specialized to particular reasoning structures or task families. In particular, Graph of States (Luo et al., 2026) is designed for abductive reasoning and couples belief representation with causal graph and state machine that explicitly constrain hypothesis evolution, making its representation closely tied to diagnosis-style tasks rather than common decision context that can be applied unchanged across all four benchmarks. Similarly, Tru-POMDP (Tang et al., 2026) assumes structured hypotheses and belief-space planning for uncertain task planning. We therefore prioritize baselines that provide representative and practically comparable alternatives to PoS under unified cross-domain evaluation protocol. D.3 Baseline Implementation Shared evaluation protocol. We evaluate all baselines through the same benchmark adapters, tool interfaces, task instructions, termination protocol, and environment-action budgets described in Appendix C. All LLM-based components follow the backbone configuration described in Appendix D.1. Because different policies naturally induce different interaction trajectories, the methods do not receive identical observations; instead, they share the same evidence-acquisition interface and differ in how the evidence produced by their own interactions is represented and exposed for subsequent decision making. Raw Trajectory, ACON, PACE, and HiAgent are integrated into common ReAct harness (Yao et al., 2023). LongHorizon-Harness retains its native ManageExecuteAudit control structure, while using the same benchmark adapters, tools, backbone, and environment-action budget. Material implementation differences. The original baselines were developed for different environments and agent protocols, so their end-to-end runners cannot be directly applied to all four benchmarks. We preserve the defining context-management mechanism of each method while adapting its interaction layer to the common benchmark interfaces. All methods receive the same task-independent background information, tool documentation, and termination instructions. Method-specific prompts contain only the instructions required to construct or operate the corresponding context representation. When an original response format is incompatible with the benchmark tool interface, we provide format demonstrations containing only interface-level examples and no evaluated cases or target answers. ACON. ACON learns compression guidelines from contrasting successful and failed trajectories and can further distill the optimized compressor (Kang et al., 2025). Our evaluation benchmarks do not provide dedicated training splits for learning such benchmark-specific compression policies, while optimizing them on evaluation cases would conflate inference-time context management with task-specific training. We therefore preserve ACONs runtime history-compression mechanism but use fixed benchmark-level preservation guidelines without failure-driven guideline optimization or compressor distillation. At each round, the Manager constructs bounded subtask from the audited task state, the Executor interacts with the environment to complete it, and the Auditor verifies the resulting state before verified requirements, artifacts, and facts are propagated to the next round. We base our implementation on the official LongHorizon-Harness codebase and preserve its native ManagerExecutorAuditor workflow and audited task-state representation. (3) Better decision context does not replace execution skills or domain knowledge. Explicit belief construction and maintenance improve how task information is represented and updated, but successful completion also depends on the models ability to act on that information. Although PoS achieves the highest success on LOCA-Benchs Env.Ops category under every backbone, performance remains between 36.00% and 41.14%. These tasks also demand reliable tool use and action sequencing, as identifying the required state change is different from executing the operations that produce it. Our ClinDiag trace analysis reveals related limitation, with many incorrect diagnoses arising after the agent receives correct information but lacks the medical knowledge needed to interpret it. Even an accurate representation of the current World State is insufficient when the agent lacks the execution skills or domain knowledge required to complete the task. Addressing these limitations requires improvements in tool-use competence and domain-specific reasoning alongside belief maintenance, rather than relying on context management alone.

sections.title: F Case Study
sections.content: We use RCA-100 case t024 with Kimi-K3 to illustrate PoSs trapping diagnosis and recovery. The agent observes abnormal inventory-service behavior but remains unable to distinguish database waiting from JVM-side processing despite continued investigation. PoS identifies Static Stagnation with persistent epistemic gap and combines constraints against ineffective repetition with requirement to seek evidence that distinguishes these explanations. The agent subsequently obtains CPU observations and integrates them with the earlier GC evidence, revising its belief and ultimately submitting the correct diagnosis. The case below traces this process from the unresolved diagnostic question to targeted recovery and belief revision. RCA-100: recovering from stalled diagnosis Case t024 Kimi-K3 The agent must identify the fault entity and failure type. This excerpt covers one of three recovery episodes in 28-action run. Step indices are zero-based. 1. Investigation continues, but the diagnostic question remains unresolved Current belief. Slow inventory requests coincide with elevated garbage-collection (GC) activity. Active epistemic gap. Are the delays caused by database waiting or processing inside the inventory JVM? Further log searches do not distinguish these explanations. Trapping diagnosis. At step 22, the same gap persists with little change in the belief. PoS identifies Belief Trapping pattern as Static Stagnation + Epistemic Gap. 2. Factorized recovery redirects investigation toward the unresolved gap Pattern constraint. Avoid repeating the ineffective action under the unchanged belief. Gap constraint. Seek evidence that distinguishes database waiting from processing inside the JVM. Agent-selected investigation. The agent chooses to inspect CPU activity. The recovery constraints specify what the investigation must resolve, rather than prescribe tool call or provide the diagnosis. 3. New evidence changes the belief and advances diagnosis New evidence. Recovery initially produces three further low-progress actions. Subsequent CPU queries reveal increased activity during the incident. Belief revision. The agent combines the CPU evidence with the earlier GC observations, increases its support for JVM-side processing, and reduces its support for database waiting. The targeted epistemic gap is recorded as resolved at step 26. Outcome. At step 27, the agent submits inventory / memoryPressure, matching both the entity and failure type in the benchmark label. Scope. The case illustrates how targeted recovery restores diagnostic progress. CPU evidence supports the recorded belief revision but does not uniquely determine the final failure type.

sections.title: G Limitations and Future Directions
sections.content: Two limitations motivate future work on the efficiency of belief maintenance and the reliability of knowledge-dependent reasoning in PoS. (1) Cost of explicit belief maintenance. The performance gains of PoS come with additional token and computational costs. Its natural language form structured Belief States require repeated text processing and generation during maintenance and subsequent reasoning. Repeatedly expressing and revising beliefs in language introduces redundancy and may cause information omission or semantic distortion. Future work could explore task-conditioned latent worldstate representations that encode decision-relevant information more compactly and support incremental updates without repeatedly expanding the state into text. The key is to encode information about the current world state in latent representation with high information density that can be efficiently propagated and updated within the model. We aim to preserve an accurate understanding of the current world state while substantially reducing the token and computational costs of belief maintenance. 26 (2) Dependence on domain and task knowledge. Although PoS receives external observations through tools, it does not systematically integrate external domain-knowledge retrieval into belief construction and reasoning. Its ability to identify relevant evidence and interpret observations therefore depends largely on the backbone models existing knowledge. Insufficient knowledge may lead to omitted facts or incorrect causal and diagnostic judgments, even when the resulting Belief State is internally consistent. Future work could incorporate domain-knowledge retrieval into belief updates and evidence interpretation, helping the agent determine what information to retain and how it supports or contradicts competing explanations. By incorporating relevant domain knowledge, we aim to improve the accuracy of Belief States and the reliability of subsequent reasoning in specialized tasks.
